You're right, and it isn't pedantry. A p-value of 0.03 is P(data this extreme or more | H0 true). The claim "97% chance the hypothesis is true" is a statement about P(hypothesis | data), which also requires a prior probability and a specific alternative. Swapping the two is the transposed-conditional fallacy.

The gap can be large. With a 50/50 prior, the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound (valid for p < 1/e under reasonable assumptions) puts the Bayes factor for H0 at no less than about 0.29 at p = 0.03. That leaves P(H0 | data) of at least roughly 22%, not 3%. With a low prior on the effect, as in exploratory work or many tested hypotheses, the posterior probability of H0 can be far higher.

Your colleague's view would be defensible only if the prior were very favorable and the test well-powered, and then the agreement would be coincidental rather than a property of p-values.
